# Introduction

s1bursts makes Sentinel-1 synthetic aperture radar (SAR) data easy to use from
Python. It searches and downloads single-look complex (SLC) data from the
[Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem](https://dataspace.copernicus.eu/) (CDSE),
processes it with [ESA SNAP](https://step.esa.int/main/toolboxes/snap/) into
backscatter and coherence, and combines the results into composites on a fixed
grid. SLC is the Sentinel-1 product that keeps the phase of the radar signal,
which coherence needs. Other products, such as ground range detected (GRD)
scenes, are not supported.

## Products

Sentinel-1's radar sends microwave pulses to the ground and records their echo,
by day and night and through clouds. s1bursts creates three products from it:

- **Backscatter** is how much of the pulse returns to the satellite. It depends
  on the roughness, moisture and structure of the surface; wet snow, for
  example, looks much darker than dry snow. Use it to follow the state of a
  surface through time.
- **Coherence** compares two acquisitions of the same place, from 0 (unrelated)
  to 1 (unchanged). It drops where the surface melted, moved, grew or was
  disturbed between the two dates. Use it to detect change.
- **Interferograms** hold the phase difference between two acquisitions and
  the intensity of each, as input for your own interferometric analysis. s1bursts does not unwrap the
  phase or estimate displacement.

Backscatter and coherence can then be combined into composites of many
acquisitions. [Products and bands](products.qmd) describes every product in
detail.

## What is a burst?

s1bursts handles Sentinel-1 data one burst at a time. A burst is the smallest
part of a Sentinel-1 scene that can be processed on its own. Each scene is made
of three strips side by side (five in EW mode), called sub-swaths, and each sub-swath is a
sequence of overlapping bursts about 20 km long. A burst download is roughly
100 MB, compared with about 4 GB for the full scene, so a study area of a few
kilometers no longer costs a whole scene.

The same footprint is imaged again on every orbit repeat, which makes bursts a
natural unit for time series. s1bursts identifies a burst by four fields:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `burst_id` | Number of the burst footprint, unique within a sub-swath |
| `sub_swath` | Sub-swath of the footprint: `IW1` to `IW3` (or `EW1` to `EW5`) |
| `polarization` | `VV`, `VH`, `HH` or `HV` |
| `date` | Acquisition time |

Together, `burst_id` and `sub_swath` name a footprint: the same patch of ground
on every repeat.

## From search to composite

A typical workflow has four steps, each handled by one class:

| Step | Class | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Search | `BurstCatalog.search()` | A `BurstCollection` of catalog records |
| Download | `BurstCatalog.download()` | One SLC file per burst |
| Process | `BurstProcessor` | One GeoTIFF per burst or burst pair |
| Composite | `ResolutionWeighter` | GeoTIFFs on 10 km MGRS grid squares |

A `FileManager` decides where every file is stored, on local disk or on S3, so
each step finds the output of the previous one.
